description: baseline

Small-n shapes (n=32/176/352) are pure launch overhead: torch.geqrf fires thousands of tiny kernels per matrix for trivial compute. Write a fused custom CUDA kernel doing one threadblock per matrix that performs the entire unblocked compact-Householder QR (geqr2) in shared memory: all n reflections, writing H (R in upper triangle, reflector vectors below the diagonal in LAPACK unit-implicit convention) and tau directly. Stream column panels through shared memory when n*n*4 exceeds smem (n=352). Eliminate per-column launches; one launch over the whole batch. Keep torch.geqrf as fallback for large n.
v1 fused geqr2 panel-tiled kernel for n in {32,176,352}; PANEL=32 all sizes. n=176 1.89x (16884->8924us), n=352 ~flat (37620->38671us), n=32 flat. geomean 112383->107404 (1.046x). All guards pass.

v2 WY/larfb blocked trailing update: larft builds T, larfb applies Q^T=I-V T^T V^T to all trailing cols as 3 GEMMs/tile (smem-tiled). n=176 8.2x->2053us, n=352 5.3x->7117us, n=32 flat 303us. geomean 82411 (1.364x). All guards pass.
Per-size tuned configs via sweep: n=176 (16,48,256)->1472us, n=352 (24,16,256)->6079us, n=32 (32,24,256)->302us. geomean 79085 (1.421x). Smaller panel wins. All guards pass.

Warp-per-column within-panel update (warp-shuffle, no per-column block sync) + retuned configs: n=32 (16,16,256)->61us, n=176 (32,32,512)->844us, n=352 (32,16,512)->4292us. geomean 64137 (1.752x). All guards pass.

Coalesced all global H accesses (row-major tile/panel load/store) + retuned: n=176 (32,48,512)->807us, n=352 (16,32,512)->3830us, n=32 (16,16,256)->60us. geomean 63393 (1.773x). ncu showed n=352 was DRAM-bound; coalescing helped. Plateau on 1-block/matrix (batch=40 blocks << 188 SMs).

Fast warp+smem block reduction for column norm (critical path). n=32 53us, n=176 737us, n=352 3670us. geomean 61974 (1.814x). Confirmed per-block latency bound (time flat batch 10..188); single-matrix critical path is the lever.

Register-blocked WY GEMMs (2 B-cols/thread, reuse shared V load -> hide smem-read stalls per ncu) + retune n=176 (24,48,512), n=352 (24,32,512). n=32 52us, n=176 639us, n=352 2825us. geomean 59698 (1.883x). All guards pass.
Widened WY GEMM register blocking to 4 B-cols/thread (more ILP hides smem-read latency). n=32 51us, n=176 605us, n=352 2611us. geomean 59195 (1.899x). All guards pass.

Tail-resident hybrid: when remaining trailing block fits smem, finish whole factorization resident in smem (warp-per-column), eliminating DRAM re-read traffic. rfit auto-capped per config. n=32 36.5us, n=176 559us, n=352 2868us. geomean 57383 (1.959x). All guards pass.

Retuned for tail-resident: n=176 (32,48,512), n=352 (16,48,512) grow the resident block (rfit~155 for n=352) -> less DRAM traffic. n=32 36us, n=176 555us, n=352 2705us. geomean 57095 (1.969x). All guards pass.

Best: geomean 57095us = 1.969x over baseline 112383 (10 successful iterations, final commit 1fe7d5b5). Built a fused one-block-per-matrix batched geqr2 for n in {32,176,352} (everything else incl. off-grid n -> torch.geqrf); all 3 anti-reward-hack guards pass every validate. Per-shape: n=32 291->36us (8x), n=176 16884->554us (30x), n=352 37620->2702us (14x). WHAT WORKED (each a commit): (1) WY/larfb blocked trailing update (larft T + B-=V(T^T(V^T B)) as tiled GEMMs) was the single biggest win - replaced per-reflector block-reductions; (2) warp-per-column within-panel update (warp-shuffle, no block sync); (3) coalesced global H access (row-major tile load/store); (4) register-blocking the WY GEMMs 4 B-cols/thread (ncu showed ~70% smem-read scoreboard stalls - this hid the latency); (5) fast warp+smem block reduction for the column norm; (6) tail-resident hybrid: once the trailing block fits smem, finish it fully resident (no DRAM re-reads), with rfit auto-capped at sqrt(front-region); (7) per-size (PANEL,TILE,threads,rfit) tuning. WHAT DIDN'T: naive #pragma unroll on the GEMM K-loops regressed (register pressure); >512 threads/block didn't help. KEY FINDING for next brief: the kernel is per-BLOCK latency-bound, not throughput-bound - total time is FLAT from batch=10..188 (one 352x352 matrix takes ~2700us whether batch is 1 or 188, since the batch=40 blocks each own an idle SM). The single-block-per-matrix design is at its ceiling. The ONLY way past it (could reach ~2.1-2.2x: n=176->~350, n=352->~1500) is MULTI-BLOCK-PER-MATRIX - split the trailing update across SMs via cooperative-groups grid sync OR a small number (~2*n/PANEL, still vastly fewer than torch.geqrf's thousands) of panel+trailing kernel launches per batch. That relaxes 'one block per matrix' but stays in spirit (kills per-column launches). Also untried: fusing the input clone() into the kernel; an n=512 fused path (batch=640 there means full GPU occupancy, so single-block-per-matrix would shine - but that shape currently goes to geqrf). NOTE: profiler (ncu/nsys) is flaky on eval.py's spawn-Pool subprocess - some captures grabbed warmup/0-smem kernels; the batch-scaling experiment was the decisive diagnostic. Scaffolding left in submission: geqr2_fused_cfg(A,panel,tile,threads,rfit) runtime entry point for fast in-process tuning sweeps (production path geqr2_fused is separate and unaffected).

Your own finding: single-block-per-matrix is latency-bound; multi-block-per-matrix is the only way past it. Worker-1 just PROVED n=4096 b=2 is 80% PANEL-bound at cuSOLVER's geqr2 floor, and the one path it identified is 'a from-scratch cooperative-groups multi-CTA batched panel beating cuSOLVER geqr2' — exactly your within-matrix-parallelism strength. Branch off the combined best 4ebf57c7. Build a cooperative-groups / multi-CTA TSQR-style panel factorization that splits each 4096-tall panel's reflector computation across MANY SMs (n=4096 has only batch=2 → 186 idle SMs), with the trailing 4096x4096 update as a big tensor-core (TF32, FP32 accumulate) GEMM. Keep V/tau FP32. NO CUDA streams (banned). Goal: beat geqrf's 40.6k on n=4096, route it into the dispatch table; leave all other n untouched, all 3 guards clean, dispatch n-keyed.

NEGATIVE RESULT (n=4096 multi-CTA panel): built a working cooperative-groups multi-CTA TSQR-style panel (grid.sync combines per-row-block partials; smem-resident panel slice; cuBLAS TF32 trailing GEMM; FP32 V/tau) -- CORRECT (passes checker + all 3 guards, compiles clean in harness) but cannot beat cuSOLVER. Best coop full-pipeline 84ms (nb16,rb48) vs geqrf 40.4ms (2.1x WORSE). Worker-2's blocked QR with cuSOLVER panel + TF32 GEMM = 42.9ms (6% worse, but it IS cuSOLVER so can't structurally beat geqrf). ROOT CAUSE measured: (1) geqrf AND blocked-QR both scale EXACTLY linearly with batch (b1=20.3ms, b2=40.5ms) -> the 2 matrices are processed serially in both, and one 4096 QR already does the bulk of the panel work; (2) trailing GEMMs are only ~5ms (TF32) -- the panel is ~85% and sits at cuSOLVER's tuned-blocked-geqr2 floor; (3) the cooperative unblocked panel pays O(nb^2) within-panel block-reductions + grid.syncs per column (grid.sync is cheap at 0.75us, but ~5 syncs x nb cols x n/nb panels = ~5n syncs + the serial per-column reduction work dominate). Beating cuSOLVER needs a from-scratch BLOCKED/recursive panel as well-tuned as cuSOLVER's -- beyond feasible scope. Per brief, left n=4096->torch.geqrf (NO regression): submission reverted to parent, geomean 7125us unchanged (parity). Coop kernel code discarded from submission to keep it minimal/low-risk for the leaderboard.

NEGATIVE RESULT on n=4096 (kept n=4096->torch.geqrf; submission == parent 4ebf57c7, geomean 7125us unchanged, no regression, all 3 guards pass). Built a complete, CORRECT cooperative-groups multi-CTA TSQR-style panel (one cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel per panel; grid.sync combines per-row-block norm/w partials; smem-resident panel slice; FP32 V/tau; cuBLAS TF32 FP32-accumulate trailing GEMM) -- it passes the checker AND all 3 anti-reward-hack guards AND compiles clean in the harness, but it is 2.1x SLOWER than geqrf (best 84ms @ nb16/rb48 vs geqrf 40.4ms). KEY MEASUREMENTS so the next worker doesn't repeat this: (a) grid.sync is cheap here (0.75us; max coop blocks 1128@256thr) -- syncs are NOT the main cost; (b) geqrf AND any blocked-QR scale EXACTLY linearly with batch (b1=20.3ms, b2=40.5ms) -> both process the 2 matrices serially, and ONE 4096 QR already does the bulk of the panel work, so 'spread across 186 idle SMs' only helps the cross-MATRIX dimension which is just 2; (c) the trailing 4096x4096 TF32 GEMMs total only ~5ms -> the panel is ~85% and sits at cuSOLVER's tuned-blocked floor; (d) worker-2's blocked QR with cuSOLVER panel + TF32 GEMM is 42.9ms (only 6% off, best nb=128) but it literally calls cuSOLVER geqrf for the panel, so it cannot structurally beat torch.geqrf (== cuSOLVER). CONCLUSION: beating cuSOLVER on n=4096 b=2 requires a from-scratch BLOCKED/recursive panel that is itself as well-tuned as cuSOLVER's internal geqr2 (an unblocked cooperative panel pays O(nb^2) within-panel reductions and loses); the win is NOT the trailing GEMM (already cheap) nor SM-occupancy (batch=2 is the only cross-matrix parallelism and geqrf is already near one-matrix latency). This corroborates worker-1's negative result. RECOMMENDATION: n=4096 is at the practical floor for this toolset -- I'd stop investing here unless someone wants to port a full communication-avoiding blocked TSQR with reflector reconstruction (high effort, uncertain payoff). Better marginal ROI is likely elsewhere (e.g. squeezing n=512/1024/2048 which dominate the geomean, or n=4096's trailing GEMM is already optimal). My brief-0 small-n kernels remain the banked win in the combine.

ONE genuinely unexplored lever for n=4096 (and maybe n=2048), the INVERSE of the multi-CTA-at-batch panel you already proved fails. Your prior attempt split the tiny batch (b=2) ACROSS CTAs -> work-starved. Instead: process the b=2 matrices SERIALLY, one at a time, giving EACH matrix ALL 188 SMs for intra-matrix parallelism, inside a SINGLE persistent cooperative-groups kernel launch that does the whole factorization with IN-KERNEL grid.sync() between reflection/panel steps - replacing the ~2n separate kernel LAUNCHES (and their fixed setup cost, which you measured dominates) with cheap in-kernel barriers. n=4096 b=2 is launch-latency + panel bound (not flop-bound: trailing GEMM already only ~5ms), so killing per-step launch overhead is exactly the lever. Panel look-ahead (overlap panel(k+1) with trailing(k)) folds into the same kernel for free. Keep genuine sequential Householder (H,tau), strictly FP32 reflectors, TF32 trailing OK. NO streams (banned). Hardest part: persistent-CTA occupancy + cooperative-launch resource limits - get a correct single matrix factoring across all SMs first, then loop the 2 matrices. Branch off best 6b928506. Goal: beat geqrf's 40.5k on n=4096; route only if it wins; all other n untouched, 3 guards clean, n-keyed. Splitting one 4096-row column across many CTAs makes each CTA's work tiny (RT=ceil(4096/RB) rows) so the barrier/reduction overhead dwarfs compute -- MORE SMs/matrix = MORE CTAs to barrier over LESS work each = slower (RB sweep: 16->162ms, 148->270ms). cuSOLVER's internal tuned blocked panel (registers/shared within optimized small kernels) is irreducibly better at the sequential thin-panel factorization than ANY grid.sync cooperative scheme. This is the 3rd independent confirmation (brief-1 batch-split 84ms, this brief single-matrix 162ms, + worker-1's negative) that n=4096 b=2 is at the cuSOLVER speed-of-light. The real wall is the per-column cross-CTA SYNC + partial-reduction COMPUTE: n=4096 = 4096 sequential Householder columns, each requiring a grid.sync (~0.75us) + a reduction over RB partials; splitting one 4096-row column across many CTAs makes per-CTA work tiny (RT=ceil(4096/RB) rows) so barrier+reduction overhead dwarfs it -- giving a matrix MORE SMs makes it SLOWER (more CTAs to barrier over less work). cuSOLVER's tuned internal blocked panel beats any grid.sync cooperative scheme at sequential thin-panel work. This is now the THIRD independent confirmation n=4096 b=2 is at cuSOLVER speed-of-light (brief-1 batch-split 84ms; this single-matrix 162ms; worker-1's prior negative). Did NOT chase n=2048 b=8 -- same per-column cooperative bottleneck, and worker-2 already does n=2048 well at 23.5ms. (2) run the diff_correctness guard (8 distinct inputs) AND a custom 20-repeat-same-object test on n=32 specifically. (3) confirm n=32 margins (factor/orth as % of budget) across many seeds + the stress cases (rankdef/clustered at n=32 if generable). (4) confirm B200-portability of the n=32 module (no gencode/sm_120). Do NOT change the kernel unless you find a real bug; if you do, fix it (correctness > the 0.44% speed). Report: is the n=32 clone-free kernel bulletproof for submission? This protects the 21.18x win.
